• Restricted-area sampling: It defines some restricted areas, within which no RSS measurements can be collected. Outside the restricted regions, RSS measurements are uniformly and randomly sampled across the accessible area. Restricted-area sampling is much more challenging than random sampling case, especially when there exists Tx inside the restricted areas.

2) Implementation Details: For the diffusion-based measurement-free RM generation model used in RadioTrace, we adopt the pre-trained model provided by RadioDiff [9], without any additional fine-tuning or retraining. The RadioDiff backbone comprises a U-Net core [22] with approximately 137M parameters and a SwinTransformer-based conditional embedding network [23] with about 87M parameters. The reverse denoising process is performed with T = 100 steps. For the Tx map generation, we set the standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel to  $ \sigma = 10 $. The Tx coordinates are optimized using momentum-based GD, with a learning rate of  $ \eta = 300 $ and a momentum coefficient of  $ \beta = 0.4 $. The upper bound of the linear scheduler of incumbent best anchor  $ \kappa = 0.8 $. The max iterations of PG-KMeans  $ L_{\max} = 10 $. The Tx coordinate set before PG-KMeans is initialized by selecting the R locations with the highest RSS values.
3) Baselines: To better contextualize the reported gains, we briefly introduce the main baselines used in our experiments.
• Kriging [11] formulates RM estimation as spatial interpolation from sparse RSS samples via a handcrafted covariance model. It does not use Tx locations or learned generative priors.

- RME-GAN [13] is a supervised, data-driven model trained offline to learn a feed-forward mapping from sparse measurements to full radio maps. It relies on large-scale training data and assumes Tx locations are available as part of the conditioning setup in our comparison. By default, RME-GAN is trained under the random sampling setting. In addition, we consider a stronger variant trained under both random and restricted-area sampling settings, denoted as RME-GAN↑, to evaluate the effect of sampling-pattern-specific supervision.

• LaPnP [17] treats RM estimation as an inverse problem by alternating between enforcing measurement consistency and applying a pre-trained latent-domain prior. Tx locations are not utilized during inference, and the prior only serves as a regularizer for map completion.

• RadioDiff-Inverse [18] treats RM construction as a diffusion-enhanced Bayesian inverse problem from noisy sparse measurements. Tx locations are not explicitly utilized during inference, and the learned diffusion prior mainly serves as a distributional regularizer rather than a Tx-geometry-aware reconstruction guide.
### C. Metrics

We evaluate reconstruction quality with four metrics: normalized mean-square error (NMSE), root-mean-square error (RMSE), structural similarity (SSIM), and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). For each test scene, we first linearly rescale the ground-truth x and predicted dB radio maps  $ \hat{x} $ to [0,1], then compute all metrics on the rescaled maps.
NMSE measures the squared error relative to the energy of the ground-truth map, providing a scale-invariant notion of distortion across scenes
$$ \mathrm{NMSE}=\frac{\|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}-\boldsymbol{x}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\boldsymbol{x}\|_{2}^{2}}. $$
RMSE is the average per-pixel deviation in the same  $ [0,1] $ units as the rescaled maps and is easy to interpret as an absolute error level
$$ \mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\hat{x}_{i}-x_{i}\right)^{2}}. $$
SSIM focuses on structural fidelity by comparing local luminance, contrast, and structure; values typically lie in  $ [0,1] $ with higher being better

$$ \mathrm{S S I M}(\boldsymbol{x},\hat{\boldsymbol{x}})=\frac{\left(2\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mu_{\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}+c_{1}\right)\left(2\sigma_{\boldsymbol{x}\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}+c_{2}\right)}{\left(\mu_{\boldsymbol{x}}^{2}+\mu_{\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}^{2}+c_{1}\right)\left(\sigma_{\boldsymbol{x}}^{2}+\sigma_{\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}}^{2}+c_{2}\right)}. $$

Here  $ \mu_{\mathbf{x}} $ and  $ \mu_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} $ are local means,  $ \sigma_{\mathbf{x}}^{2} $ and  $ \sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}^{2} $ are local variances,  $ \sigma_{\mathbf{x}\hat{\mathbf{x}}} $ is the local covariance, and  $ c_{1}, c_{2} $ are stabilization constants.
PSNR expresses fidelity in decibels as a monotonic transform of MSE; with maps rescaled to  $ [0,1] $, larger PSNR directly corresponds to smaller MSE
$$ \mathrm{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{MSE}}\right). $$
The metrics are computed over all pixels per scene and then averaged over the test set.
